paras: The lynching of a gambler at Baldwin, Florida, was a killing at some point before March 1881 that the Tallahassee Economist described as 'a visitation from Judge Lynch' upon the gamblers who worked from the town. It is known only from a passing reference in a Florida editorial on railroad swindlers, which gives no date, name or race for the man killed.

Baldwin stood at 'the point of intersection of the two railroads', and the Economist described it as the headquarters of the gamblers from whom 'the travelling public' most suffered. From there, according to the paper, they plied their trade on the railroads, and the 'notoriety of their swindling operations' was 'a reproach to Florida justice'.

The Economist wrote that the gamblers had received a warning 'some time since' in the form of a 'visitation from Judge Lynch, when one of their number was killed.' The coverage gives no account of who carried out the killing, how many took part, how the man died, or what, if anything, he personally was accused of.
By the Economist's account the killing had little effect, since the gamblers went on working 'but little if at all deterred'. No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The only surviving mention is a reprint of the Economist editorial in the 'Florida Affairs' column of the Savannah Morning News on 16 March 1881, set among items on crops, railroads and crime. The Economist raised the lynching to argue about remedies for railroad swindling, calling Lynch law 'one of the worst of evils, and only justifiable, if at all, when there is no other adequate remedy.' It concluded instead that the railroads should refuse to carry 'sharpers and swindlers' known to their employees, and the Savannah paper added no comment of its own.

bases: The only report describes the killing of a Baldwin gambler as 'a visitation from Judge Lynch' and links it to 'Lynch law' (A1).

The Tallahassee Economist, as quoted, says one gambler was killed in a 'visitation from Judge Lynch' meant as a 'warning' to the gamblers, which implies an extralegal killing under a pretext of justice (A1); no report gives the number of killers, the victim's name or race, or the date.
One passing back-reference in a Florida news column, quoting one Florida paper, is the only report found (A1).

accounts.label: Tallahassee Economist editorial (as quoted)
accounts.gist: In an editorial on railroad gamblers, the Economist mentions in passing that the Baldwin gamblers had received a warning 'in the shape of a visitation from Judge Lynch, when one of their number was killed.'

framing.detail: The Economist treats the killing as an ineffective 'warning' to swindlers, calls Lynch law 'one of the worst of evils' but 'justifiable, if at all' when no other remedy exists, and urges the railroads to refuse to carry known sharpers; the Savannah Morning News reprints it without comment.
